draft.title: Adding and scaling matrices
card: The order of a matrix is its number of rows × its number of columns. Two matrices can be added only if they have the same order.
Adding
add the elements in the same position. For example, [2 5] + [3 −1] = [5 4].
Scalar multiplication
a scalar is an ordinary number. To multiply a matrix by it, multiply every element. For example, 3 × [2 −4] = [6 −12].
Subtracting works the same way as adding. Take away the element in the same position, and watch the signs.
draft.remember: Add matching positions. A scalar multiplies every element.

a.why: First, 2 × [3 −5] = [6 −10]. Then add [1 4] to get [7 −6]. Multiplying only the first element by 2 would give [7 −1], but a scalar multiplies every element.
a.clue: Scale first, then add matching positions.

b.q: Mia's café sells these items on two days. Monday: 12 coffees, 8 muffins. Tuesday: 15 coffees, 6 muffins. She expects next week's sales to be 3 times the total of these two days. How many muffins does she expect?
b.why: Total muffins over the two days is 8 + 6 = 14. Multiplying by 3 gives 42. The answer 14 stops before the scalar step.
b.clue: Add the two days first, then multiply the muffin total.

problems.detail: The question does not set out any matrix, so students can answer with plain arithmetic (8 + 6 = 14, then × 3) and it does not test matrix addition or scaling. Its sales-by-day setting also leans into point 5 (Matrices in context). Showing the two days as row matrices, such as [12 8] + [15 6], would tie it to this point.

check.summary: Both answers check out: [7 −6] for a and 42 for b, and the explanations are correct. Question b can be solved without matrices and overlaps with the 'Matrices in context' point, so it should present the data as matrices.

proposal.title: Adding and scaling matrices
card: The order of a matrix is its number of rows × its number of columns. Two matrices can be added only if they have the same order.
Adding
add the elements in the same position. For example, [2 5] + [3 −1] = [5 4].

Subtracting works the same way as adding. Take away the element in the same position, and watch the signs.
proposal.remember: Add matching positions. A scalar multiplies every element.

a.why: First, 2 × [3 −5] = [6 −10]. Then add [1 4] to get [7 −6]. Multiplying only the first element by 2 would give [7 −1], but a scalar multiplies every element.
a.clue: Scale first, then add matching positions.

b.q: A = [5 −3] and B = [2 4]. What is 2 × (A − B)?
b.why: A − B = [5 − 2 −3 − 4] = [3 −7], and 2 × [3 −7] = [6 −14]. The answer [8 −10] comes from 2A − B, which doubles A but not B. The scalar multiplies the whole bracket.
b.clue: Work out the bracket first, and watch the sign of −3 − 4.

final.title: Adding and scaling matrices
card: The order of a matrix is its number of rows \(\times\) its number of columns. Two matrices can be added only if they have the same order.
Adding
add the elements in the same position. For example, \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).
Scalar multiplication
a scalar is an ordinary number. To multiply a matrix by it, multiply every element. For example, \(3 \times \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -12 \end{bmatrix}\).
Subtracting works the same way as adding. Take away the element in the same position, and watch the signs.
final.remember: Add matching positions. A scalar multiplies every element.

a.why: First, \(2 \times \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -10 \end{bmatrix}\). Then add \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) to get \(\begin{bmatrix} 7 & -6 \end{bmatrix}\). Multiplying only the first element by 2 would give \(\begin{bmatrix} 7 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), but a scalar multiplies every element.
a.clue: Scale first, then add matching positions.

b.why: \(A - B = \begin{bmatrix} 5 - 2 & -3 - 4 \end{bmatrix}\), which is \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -7 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(2 \times \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -14 \end{bmatrix}\). The answer \(\begin{bmatrix} 8 & -10 \end{bmatrix}\) comes from \(2A - B\), which doubles \(A\) but not \(B\). The scalar multiplies the whole bracket.
b.clue: Work out the bracket first, and watch the sign of \(-3 - 4\).
